cases.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: arccotangent of 2 in radians
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.4636. Independently verified: acot(2) = atan(1/2) = 0.4636476090008061 -> 0.4636 at 4 dp. (Excel's ACOT returns the principal value in 0..pi, which for a positive argument agrees with atan(1/x))

cases.description: The arccotangent of zero, the midpoint of the documented 0..pi output range
cases.expected_note: Excel documents "The returned angle is given in radians in the range 0 (zero) to pi", and cot(pi/2) = 0, so ACOT(0) = pi/2. Independently verified: math.pi/2 = 1.5707963267948966 -> 1.570796327 at 9 dp. This case distinguishes the documented 0..pi principal branch from the atan(1/x) shortcut, which is undefined at 0

cases.description: A negative argument, where the documented 0..pi range differs from atan(1/x)
cases.expected_note: Excel documents the result is in the range 0 to pi, so for a negative argument ACOT(-2) = pi + atan(1/-2) = pi - 0.4636476090008061 = 2.677945044588987 -> 2.677945045 at 9 dp, NOT the negative -0.4636 that atan(1/x) alone would give

cases.description: Arccotangent of -0.5, a negative argument between -1 and 0
cases.expected_note: Microsoft documents "The returned angle is given in radians in the range 0 (zero) to pi", so for a negative argument the result is pi + atan(1/x), not atan(1/x) alone: ACOT(-0.5) = pi + atan(1/-0.5) = pi + atan(-2) = 3.141592653589793 - 1.1071487177940904 = 2.0344439357957027 -> 2.034443936 at 9 dp. The bare atan(1/x) shortcut would give -1.107148718, which is pi lower and outside the documented 0..pi range

cases.description: Arccotangent of -1, the mirror of the documented ACOT(1) = pi/4 example
cases.expected_note: Microsoft documents "The returned angle is given in radians in the range 0 (zero) to pi", so ACOT(-1) = pi + atan(1/-1) = pi - pi/4 = 3*pi/4 = 2.356194490192345 -> 2.35619449 at 9 dp. cot(3*pi/4) = -1, confirming the value is a genuine arccotangent and not merely a sign flip of ACOT(1); the bare atan(1/x) shortcut would give -0.785398163, exactly pi lower

cases.description: Arccotangent of -10, a large negative argument approaching the top of the documented range
cases.expected_note: Microsoft documents "The returned angle is given in radians in the range 0 (zero) to pi", so ACOT(-10) = pi + atan(1/-10) = 3.141592653589793 - 0.09966865249116204 = 3.0419240010986313 -> 3.041924001 at 9 dp. As x -> -infinity the documented branch approaches pi from below; the bare atan(1/x) shortcut would give -0.099668652, approaching 0 from below instead

cases.description: The same negative-argument arccotangent converted to degrees, where the branch choice is a 180 degree difference
cases.expected_note: Microsoft documents "The returned angle is given in radians in the range 0 (zero) to pi" and points to DEGREES for the conversion, so DEGREES(ACOT(-1)) = DEGREES(pi + atan(1/-1)) = DEGREES(3*pi/4) = 135 exactly. An engine that returns the bare atan(1/x) instead reports -45 degrees for the same cell, i.e. the same direction rotated by 180 degrees

cases.description: Arccotangent of 1, the positive control where every convention agrees
cases.expected_note: Microsoft documents "The returned angle is given in radians in the range 0 (zero) to pi". For a positive argument pi + atan(1/x) would fall outside 0..pi, so the documented branch is plain atan(1/x): ACOT(1) = atan(1) = pi/4 = 0.7853981633974483 -> 0.785398163 at 9 dp. LibreOffice documents the same value for this exact formula ("=ACOT(1) returns 0.785398163397448 (PI/4 radians)"). This is the control case: it isolates the divergence to negative arguments
Excel documents: "If Number is a non-numeric value, ACOT returns the #VALUE! error value."
